protections: Per-attribute allowlists: every attribute on a validated element is checked against the policy in the DOM scanner (processAttributes) and the SAX scanner (startElement loop) before it reaches output.
CSS allowlist: <style> text and style attribute values are parsed by Batik and validated property-by-property by CssValidator/CssHandler in both scanners.
URL allowlist: URI-bearing attribute values and CSS url() values are constrained by the onsiteURL/offsiteURL/anchoredURL policy regular expressions.

Serialization guards: URI attribute values are escaped by the serializer (ASHTMLSerializer.escapeURI), text/CDATA is entity-encoded, and empty non-void elements get closing tags through require-closing-tags (ASXHTMLSerializer).

Parser configuration: each NekoHTML parser is configured for its scan mode (DOM: lowercased element names, CDATA sections, strict attribute names; SAX: fragment balancing, CDATA sections, character-reference notifications).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The DOM parser already enables strict attribute names and the SAX path is assumed to inherit strictness from the XML parser layer, so the missing setFeature call looks redundant.
NekoHTML is assumed to return one text child for <style> content, and any element children are still walked by processChildren, so reading only the first child is taken to cover the element's CSS.

The XHTML serializer inherits XML-correct attribute escaping from its base class, so the escapeURI override that HTML output needed is assumed unnecessary in the XHTML output path (which the default policy selects).
A backslash makes the value a relative path rather than a protocol-relative URL, and the observable effect is open redirect or dangling markup, not script execution.
The shipped policies remove script and iframe, and HTML output already emits explicit closing tags for non-void elements, so a three-entry default require-closing list is assumed sufficient.

fairness_risks: A strict rule that rejects <style> elements with mixed or multiple children (the natural T2 fix) also refuses legacy markup that wraps CSS in HTML comments inside <style>, which the sanitizer currently accepts.
Extending require-closing-tags (T5) must not force closing tags onto genuinely void elements (br, img, hr, input, meta, link) or legitimate serialized markup and its parity tests change.
Removing the backslash from onsiteURL (the natural T4 fix) also refuses relative URLs containing backslashes that applications may legitimately feed through href, background and usemap.

Enabling strict attribute names on the SAX parser (the natural T1 fix) can reject attribute names that browsers tolerate and that custom policies deliberately allow, so parity with the DOM parser must be checked against must-keep-working policies.

The refused input shape for T2 -- a <style> element whose content is split into several text/markup nodes -- is produced by some editors and by the select/option parsing path, so a blanket rejection is not obviously safe.

design.why: The four traps occupy four different fix sites and carry four different dismissals: T2 is the DOM-only half of the <style>-content guard (the SAX sibling validates every character), T1 is parser hardening present only in the DOM parser configuration, T3 is the URI-escape guard present in the HTML serializer but absent from the XHTML sibling that the default policy selects, and T4 is a lexical URL-allowlist shape that the existing protocol-relative guard does not cover. They span both scan implementations, both serializers and the policy layer; they include deepseek-type absent-guard routes (T1, T3) and how-type/coupled shapes (T2, T4), so fixing one path or over-hardening one layer still leaves a hidden test failing. T5 is recorded as a fifth independent group but excluded from the design because its impact depends on custom policies validating script/iframe.
